what_it_does: Recommendation models — the AI systems that suggest products, videos, or ads — store huge lookup tables called embedding tables that can reach terabyte scale, far too large to fit in ordinary fast memory (DRAM). Tiered memory systems address this by pairing a smaller amount of fast DRAM with a larger amount of slower, cheaper memory, but the trick is knowing which embedding entries to keep in the fast tier. Standard caching rules (like 'keep recently used items') fail here because recommendation lookups are sparse and irregular, with very long and unpredictable gaps between reuses. RecMG trains separate small machine-learning models to make these placement decisions: one model predicts which entries are unlikely to be needed again soon and can be moved to slow memory, and another predicts which entries to fetch early from slow memory before they are needed. Both models are tailored to the unusual access patterns of recommendation workloads, reducing costly on-demand fetches from slow memory.
